newsitem.title: RWANDA: U.N. workers in Rwanda await army protection plans.
newsitem.headline: U.N. workers in Rwanda await army protection plans.

text.p: U.N. personnel have been withdrawn from western Rwanda while plans are made for army protection of U.N. staff, vehicles and their bases after a wave of killings of foreigners, aid workers said on Thursday.

"We are in negotiations with the Rwandan government about exactly what security measures are to be implemented involving the use of Rwandan government soldiers to protect U.N. vehicles, personnel and compounds," said U.N. spokesman John McMillan.
He gave no details but aid officials said non-essential U.N. staff were leaving temporarily for Kenya's capital Nairobi and all U.N. aid workers in western Rwanda had been pulled back to Kigali.
U.N. staff were placed on "security level four", meaning essential aid operations would continue but non-essential travel was cancelled, U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said in New York on Wednesday.

Attackers ambushed and killed four U.N. human rights monitors near the southwestern town of Cyangugu on Tuesday. Their Rwandan driver was wounded and later died. Few details were released but aid sources said they were hacked to pieces and one had been beheaded.
The bodies of British and Cambodian monitors, 36-year-old Graham Turnbull of York, England, and 34-year-old Saspra Chim Chan of Cambodia, were flown to Nairobi, Kenya, from Kigali on Wednesday.
Two Rwandan monitors were killed with them on a visit in a marked U.N. vehicle in the southwest, which borders on Zaire.
Non-U.N. agencies suspended their work in Rwanda after the killings or pulled their expatriates out of the west and back to the capital. They imposed an evening to dawn curfew on staff.
Aid officials said non-U.N. aid agencies met on Thursday but they doubted they would reach a concensus on security measures.

There have been eight attacks on expatriates in Rwanda in the last three weeks, putting at risk aid agency efforts to help Rwanda after its 1994 genocide and the return of more than one million Hutu refugees from Zaire and Tanzania late last year.

Three Spanish aid workers were killed in cold blood in the northwestern town of Ruhengeri on January 18 by suspected Hutu militiamen. A 61-year-old Canadian missionary was shot dead by a lone gunman on Sunday in a church in Ruhengeri prefecture.
Following Tuesday's killings, The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) halted work for 10 days. The international federation of Red Cross societies reduced to an emergency staff.

"The ICRC will have 10 days of reflection after the multiplication of attacks on expatriates in Rwanda," said ICRC spokesman Josue Anselmo in Kigali on Thursday. "But the two main problems remain which is how to provide aid but at the same time ensure the security of our staff."

"Our operations have been frozen and non-essential personnel have been put on standby in Nairobi. However our sub-delegations countrywide will be remaining in position but they will not work apart from supplying life-saving aid," he said.
Rwandan officials said government ministers may have been the targets of Tuesday's ambush because they were in the area on a tour trying to reconcile the Hutu majority and Tutsi minority.

The U.N. Human Rights Operation in Rwanda reported on Friday Hutu death squads were killing Tutsi genocide survivors and witnesses to the slaughter, apparently to stop them denouncing people for the 1994 ethnic bloodbath of some 800,000 people.
